utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. There are a few procedural matters which can be dealt with right away in your presence, Mr. Krajisnik, now -- I've not reminded you yet as a witness to the solemn declaration, so at this moment you're still the accused and not the witness in your case. First of all, the Judges would decide on whether they would agree with the alternative option for contacting your counsel not by letter but by raising the matter in open court. Of course, as an alternative option, I mean, if you'd like to do it by letter, that's still possible. We have taken notice of the concerns of communication with counsel; we'll take care of that. And we did not understand that there would be any objection from the Prosecution. There is not, so therefore as an alternative option, you are allowed to do so. I even was informed that your first application would be made soon, perhaps even very soon. But before we allow you to make such an application, there is another matter, which is P1135. We do understand, Mr. Josse, that you have agreed that the whole of that document could be admitted into evidence but that you'd like to clearly have on the record that it is without prejudice to the -- to the position of the Defence on a similar point in the future. That's on the record now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, therefore, P1135 is now in its entirety admitted into evidence. As far as D171 and 173 is concerned, later today an opportunity will be given to briefly and in private session address the request to have these two exhibits admitted under seal. Then as far as D146 is concerned, the minutes of the 77th Session of the Bosnian Presidency, it was tendered on the 16th of March and the English translation was received on the 26th of April. If the Prosecution would have taken already a position as far as whether it should be objected or not, I'd like to hear; if not, the Chamber would like to hear that by next Monday. Yes. And I always make mistakes by using the word "next." The Monday to come after this weekend.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that -- if I'm not mistaken, that may be a holiday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, you're right. I'm not -- yes. It's good that foreigners remind me that on the 1st of May we celebrate the birthday of our Queen, although it's not the day of her birthday. It was, just for your information, inherited from her mother who celebrated her birthday on the 31st of April. Then that will then be Tuesday, Mr. Tieger. D139, I do understand that the Defence was ordered on the 16th of March to submit a CD and a B/C/S transcript by the 27th of March and that an English transcript was finally provided on the 4th of April, that filing -- for filing a deadline was set 28th of April and that you're now ready to submit D139.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm told that that's been done, I'm glad to say, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it's in the hands of Mr. Registrar, and it's -- were there any objections? I don't remember. I think it was not complete, but could we also hear by Tuesday whether there are any objections against admission of D139. Then I dealt with the procedural issues. Mr. Krajisnik, now you are a witness again in your own case, and as a witness I do understand that you wanted to raise an issue of contact with -- contact with counsel. Of course then that would be accused/counsel contact. You may address the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to speak to my lawyer briefly to consult about what I wish to present here in court and which is not related to my testimony, not directly but indirectly. It has to do with the information provided in the media in Bosnia-Herzegovina which is not appropriate and which is damaging this trial, myself, and my family terribly. So that's why I'm asking you this. I know that I'm prohibited from talking to them or to anyone else. I didn't know how to address the issue. I thought that I should speak to him on this matter and then either I should address the Court or he should address the Court. Perhaps I think it's better if Mr. Stewart addresses the Court on that matter, if you allow me to consult him. If that is not possible, I would like to ask you to allow me to address you myself. I know what you said and I would like to abide by it fully to honour what the usual practice is, and I want to exercise full discipline. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for our better understanding, Mr. Krajisnik, do I understand you well, and the Judges will consider your request during the next break, but do I understand you well that when you talk about information in the media in Bosnia-Herzegovina that it's information about your testimony? Or do I not understand you well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has to do with misinterpreting what I said here before this Court, and that has been causing the wrong kind of consequences in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's why I would like to consult my lawyer. I think that what you said is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And if you say "what I said here in court," you mean to refer to what you said as a witness in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no -- oh, yes, yes, as a witness. Yesterday and the day before yesterday. I cannot remember the days right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that's perfectly clear. We'll consider the matter over the next break and we come with a decision --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- when possible. Yes, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just wondering whether as Mr. Krajisnik's counsel whether briefly I could make a comment before Your Honours consider it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we suggest, although we're in Your Honours' hands, we suggest that probably and based on past experience in related matters, it probably would be helpful to the Trial Chamber and all concerned if it were felt appropriate to allow Mr. Krajisnik to speak to us first and just, if you like, sift and identify what the issue is, what the channels of communication have been in relation to this matter, because obviously Mr. Krajisnik has obtained this information from Bosnia. We know nothing about that at the moment, Your Honour. And also for the future, it may be that we can establish different or other lines of communication which would help to smooth this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I -- so what you would say, actually, Mr. Stewart is that you would prefer that permission would be granted to Mr. Krajisnik to speak about it rather than him addressing the Chamber on the matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that would seem likely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was your primary --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. So we support that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll consider it and most likely after the first break give a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But of course I can't promise anything because we have to conclude our deliberations on the matter, but we'll try to do our utmost best. Then, Mr. Krajisnik, this is the moment that I'm going to remind you, as I did, as you may have noticed, with all witnesses, I'm going to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration given at the beginning of your testimony. And, Mr. Stewart, I don't know whether it's you or whether it's Mr. Josse, who will continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm simply going to deal with one other intercept, Your Honour, which follows on from the one that was dealt with yesterday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I'm going to deal with what is P396, an intercept that was dealt with during the evidence of Mr. Bjelobrk. It has been played for the Court already. I do not intend to have it replayed now. The interpreters have copies. I have some others here -- first of all, could Mr. Krajisnik have one in his language. I don't know who else would like a copy. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two of the Judges have it and I have to -- yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, here's one for you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I've got it. I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I notified the Chamber this morning that it was going to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. We all have it in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, yesterday you were dealing with the historical agreement and the Belgrade Initiative. This was another conversation with Mr. Karadzic on that subject. In the English I would invite everyone to turn to the bottom of page 2 where it says -- where Dr. Karadzic says: "Now they will, we will have the initiative, they will have to explain to their people what they want if they don't want this."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK SAYS
utterances.text: "Yes. What is it really, if they don't want this, what do they want?" Karadzic: "He wants to force Tudjman, so let's force Tudjman, we don't mind." Krajisnik: "Nobody is stopping him." Karadzic: "We don't mind forcing Tudjman to accept this. Krajisnik: "Yes. Karadzic: "We will not force him. Krajisnik: "So I said please. I fought for the republic to be equal in the end. I stress I really took care not to break any regulation from the agreement of the Muslims and the Serbs." Two or three lines on then. Mr. Krajisnik: "I don't care about the others, I said it deliberately. Not one ... Equal republic, integral with the same status, I would not let Bosnia have a different status." Firstly, is this a reference --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. -- we, as we were requested to do, brought our copy of P396. I notice that from what you're reading there are some differences, I would say minor ones, but it seems as if we're working from a different -- let me just see whether I have the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This is a constant problem, Your Honour. It's a problem in relation to other documents. And Mr. Stewart and I came across the same problem this morning in relation to a -- some Assembly sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but if you're quoting from an exhibit which was admitted, then of course we'd like you to quote from that version of the document. I think as far as the portions read are concerned, there are no major differences, apart from that where it reads: "And that we are all treated the same," that the words "the same status is used. I would not let Bosnia," here it says "be treated differently," and here I think you just read "have a different status." So there are minor -- I wouldn't say that -- one couldn't even say that one contradicts the other, but the translation is phrased in a different way. Let's proceed for the time being because I don't think it really affects your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The extract that I have just read, Mr. Krajisnik, refers to what negotiations, please?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were the negotiations that were held in Belgrade and that have to do with the Belgrade Initiative. They were relying upon the historic agreement between the Serbs and Muslims. The Belgrade Initiative came as a result of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what stance are you enunciating here to Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm complaining, in a way, to Mr. Karadzic to the effect that objections were raised against me because I was in favour of this Belgrade Initiative, although I insisted that everything in this document should be as envisaged in the historic agreement and that it should, in fact, be incorporated in the Belgrade Initiative. I did not allow Bosnia not to be equal, so I did everything that Mr. Zulfikarpasic and Mr. Filipovic had asked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I want to ask you about one other passage a few lines further down where there is some reference to Alija. Where Dr. Karadzic says: "Maybe you fought more than Alija would." You laugh and say: "I see it's" -- let me correct that. In the version that I've very helpfully been provided by the registrar, the English is: "Maybe you obtained more through the struggle than Alija would have." Your response is: "I see it's better to send me than Alija because these Serbs think he would not ... I would not trick them. Well, let it be, we want it honest, it doesn't matter." Karadzic: "Yes, yes. I mean, now we can only be surprised and they, like, they are aggressive. Let them be aggressive now, let their people see what they, what they want, so do you people want, if you don't want this." What's being said there between the two of you, please?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was a lot younger then and my nerves or a lot better. Even the most serious matters were things that I had a relaxed attitude about. See, even this serious matter here that perhaps I handled it better than Alija would have, I even put that in a slightly humourous way, but the point was that even had the late Alija Izetbegovic, who advocated -- even if the late Alija Izetbegovic had participated in the negotiations, he would not have advocated the Bosnian cause better. So that was said my way of a joke, but the point was to say that I achieved more than even Alija Izetbegovic would have achieved had he been at that meeting. But the form is, well, sort of, I always wanted to talk to people that way, not on the basis of tensions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's all I want to ask on this topic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm going to turn to the Serb Assembly Session of the 24th of October, 1991. I think that notification was given that this was an item that we would be going to more or less straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we have an exhibit number for that? I don't -- as a matter of fact, I remember that we have supposed to bring the A and B instructions. We were requested --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, we gave advance notice of that, in effect, Your Honour, because we don't expect actually to get to those today, but that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but not the session -- you're now referring to the 24th of October -- oh, that's perhaps the -- yes. I do understand it's P64A, tab 270. I can at least find it on my computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Your Honour. Yes, that's the correct document. That's the -- that's the one notified and it is the right one. And, Your Honour, I've got in accordance with the practice yesterday, I have a B/C/S copy with those similar marginal numbering notes but no other notes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters please have copies. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Please have copies or have? Exactly the same, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We have not received any documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I thought --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The English booth does not have a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's discrimination between the different languages. I do understand.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, if it could help, perhaps the document could be placed on the ELMO. But as a rule three copies are needed, one per each booth. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that one copy was provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I've got another copy, Your Honour. It doesn't have that marginal numbering, but that shouldn't be a major difficulty if we just get the page number as we go through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, or be put on the ELMO so that both booths would have --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we might be able to assist. We have additional copies as well. They can be returned to us after they're used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If then perhaps an English version could be put on the ELMO so the Judges have access to it on their screens, all of us, unless there's another English copy available.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We can put the English on your screens, Your Honour, through Mr. Sladojevic, in the way we did yesterday. The only remaining question is whether anybody then needs the English on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think we would then need it and I -- okay. Let's try to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. And one presses the middle left button on that mini console, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We seem to be in business, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you should have in front of you a copy in your own language of a transcript of the Serb Assembly held on the 24th of October, 1991, and we're going to operate the -- broadly the same system as yesterday with the marginal numbering. You're familiar with that by now. Could you find number 1? It's only about three or four pages into the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, in the English it's on page 6 where Mr. Krajisnik is shown as starting to speak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. "Ladies and gentlemen," and so on, you say. "The club of Serbian representatives in the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina gave me the honour to speak on their behalf. First of all, I would like to inform the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the entire Serbian people everywhere, the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as well as the Yugoslav and world public, about the reasons why the Serbian representatives in the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina have decided to establish the Assembly of Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina and about their rights and the significance and tasks of this Assembly." Mr. Krajisnik, just to put it in its context - and we've had lots of evidence about it and I'm not going to explore the topic with you - this of course followed a matter of nine days after the crisis in the Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly when the Serb deputies left the chamber, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then you continue here: "The main reason lies in a serious attempt to compromise the national sovereignty of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina and their constitutional and legal position in Yugoslavia, which in turn compromises their survival in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, where they have lived from time immemorial." Mr. Krajisnik, can we -- when you were saying "in turn compromises their survival in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina," were you intending that literally in the sense of their continuing to live and exist in that territory?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could not be taken literally, so it's not that literally. It was used in a pejorative sense. I can even explain that if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm wondering if the word that came across in the English translation was "pejorative." I only --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: That was said in the B/C/S, notes the interpreter, "pejorative."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From what my guess would be, if I compare to other languages I know, it's saying things -- things being worse than they actually are. "Peior" is Latin for worse, from what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm in a position to confirm that from my own knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if we understand it this way. I don't know whether it's English which is usually --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, I did question it only because in English it simply has the sense of being in some way insulting or -- so I questioned it because it doesn't fit very well in English at all. Mr. Harmon is nodding. We don't always agree linguistically across the Atlantic, but here we do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would be good if you could ask Mr. Krajisnik to clarify exactly what he meant when he used that word in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's what I had in mind, Your Honour. I didn't want to comment on it inappropriately.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, perhaps -- you weren't using it literally -- well, in some sense then I'll put -- in some sense you were using it figuratively. What in fact did you have in -- what were you intending to convey?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said this sentence, I meant that the Serb people were a constituent people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the three equal peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina. If Bosnia-Herzegovina were to become a unitary state and if we would accept for the Serb people not to be a constituent people, then in fact they would turn into a minority, and then the survival of the Serb people would be brought into question because you have certain rights as a people, and when you are a national minority then you have less rights. When I use the word "pejorative," I was trying to say that I was not speaking literally. It's not that everybody would not survive. I was just trying to say that their rights would be jeopardised, that some of their rights would be denied. That is what I meant, although "pejorative" may mean something different in your language.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, that's -- thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. The -- then further on -- I'm not going to read the whole of this answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, sometimes if I don't do that in the interests of saving time, may I nevertheless particularly invite Your Honours to -- to note that passage. This is Mr. Krajisnik speaking rather than I simply taking the time to go through it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, then I pick it up again then. It's page 8 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But, Mr. Krajisnik, it's about three or four large paragraphs further on where it says in the English: "At this point there is no need to spend more time ..." Completely apposite phrase. "At this point there is no need to spend more time on the constitutional amendments ..." Do you have that? You're nodding. "At this point there is no need to spend more time on the constitutional amendments which were adopted by the former parliament, in collaboration with our partners in the government at the end of the mandate. In one of those amendments, the inalienable sovereignty was transferred from the people to the republic, which is contrary to the federal constitution." Now, what -- what did you have specifically in mind there, Mr. Krajisnik, by talking of transfer from the people to the republic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You can see it. We have it here as an exhibit from the Prosecution, and in this constitution it says that sovereignty is at the level of the people -- the peoples, Muslims, Croats, and Serbs. The amendments that were introduced at the last moment divided this sovereignty. So it was at the level of the republic, but in part it also belonged to the peoples. So the status of the rights of the peoples deteriorated, not only the Serbs but all three. So, in a way, it became debatable, if I can put it that way. So that was done on the eve of the multi-party elections at the last moment by the former Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then you continue in the next paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours, I'm not going to read that paragraph but simply invite Your Honours to note that as part of Mr. Krajisnik's contribution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then there's a paragraph, middle of page 9 of the English, you begin: "In addition to all this ..." Do you see that paragraph, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "In addition to all this, the present structure of the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina does not include a constitutional and legal institution which would protect each of the three constituent peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina from being out-voted. True, in the essential rights of the national groups, an amendment to the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina of 1990 introduced the Council for National Equality, which was to decide on such issues by a consensus. However, the Council has not been established to this day. Although the draft of the code on the Council entered the parliament procedure several months ago, the code has not been adopted yet simply because the coalition of the SDA and the HDZ opposes its authorities granted by the constitution." Again, Mr. Krajisnik, I'm not going to go into the technicalities and constitutional aspects of that with you, but just invite you to confirm, if you can. That issue about the Council of National Equality, that had been in the nature of a running saw or continuing issue of conflict, hadn't it, between the Serbs in the parliament on the one hand and the Muslims and Croats on the other?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a constant subject of debate among us, but the answer to your question is: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then do you see a marginal note 3. It's just about a page or so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's at page 11 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you see that, Mr. Krajisnik, number 3. Just going a few lines above where it should be marked there's a sentence that begins: "For example, the republican MUP." Do you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There's a reference in the same sentence to the SDA/HDZ coalition. Do you see that? It should be just about three or four lines up from where you see the number 3 in the margin.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't find the words "MUP" anywhere in the Serbian version. I found the representative of the HDZ --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour -- yes, I don't know what's happening, Your Honour. It's -- Your Honour, we could very quickly offer assistance in identifying the sentence, I'm sure. It's unusual for Mr. Krajisnik to need it, but if -- something is clearly going wrong ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I got it. It's a bit lower, not above, number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, I'm -- the number 3 has slipped then. My apologies, Mr. Krajisnik, and sometimes the print isn't that distinct either. The -- all right. You've got it then. Well, I'll read the sentence: "In that way, some laws, decisions, and regulations which are unconstitutional and against the vital interests of the Serbian people in many areas are imposed upon them. For example, the republican MUP is in the hands of the SDA/HDZ coalition and there are indications that the enormous increase in the number of police reservists, feverish technical equipping and arming of the police have in fact been carried out in order to create a special army in Bosnia and Herzegovina." Mr. Krajisnik, you refer to indications. Could you describe the nature of the indications which you were aware of at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was always cautious in sharing the information that I had. I always tried to avoid outright assertions. But this was common knowledge that a decision was made to level out, as they say, the ethnic force and to mobilise a lot of men from the Croat and Muslim ranks. And that did produce an impression that the MUP was being reinforced and equipped in order to create a Muslim army. I did not want to -- to say that in so many words. I wanted everyone to have their own opinion, but it was a fact that a great number of reservists had been mobilised in a number of municipalities and it was a fact that the greatest number of them was Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then you continue: "The instruction by the defence minister regarding the list of conscripts and his orders that the men of military age and reservists should not respond to the call-up represent examples of flagrant violation of the federal and republican law with the aim of instilling disorder in Bosnia and Herzegovina." First of all, the defence minister at that time was who?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Mr. Doko, Jerko Doko.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the call-up being referred to there was call-up to the JNA, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That, I think, should be an invitation to national defence secretariats across municipalities. If you allow me to read. "The instructions of the minister of defence regarding lists," this is a reference to the secretariats of national defence which held lists of men, according to which conscription was carried out. Maybe I should read it more carefully. The demand from the army was that they wanted to take-over those lists and take-over mobilisation as such, because the secretariats of national defence did not want to perform their duty to carry out mobilisation, as envisaged by the federal law, according to the instructions given by the minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You can turn on quite a lot of pages now, Mr. Krajisnik, please, probably about 10 in your copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, this goes to page 25 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, what we're looking for is a number 4 in the margin and it should be very close to something headed "decision for the Serbian people to stay in a joint state of Yugoslavia." Let us know, please, when you've found that.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, and against that or very close to that do you see the heading: "Decision for the Serbian people to stay in a joint state of Yugoslavia"?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It's page 21 in the Serbian version, if that could help the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It would. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, page 21.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was about to praise the good organisation, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I would have welcomed that rare accolade from you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm confident, Mr. Krajisnik, that you'll find another opportunity to do so in the near future.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you go and have a look where that is in their version -- I found it, actually, in my copy, even without the number. But it's before the 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I -- Mr. Krajisnik, we've identified the mild breakdown in the system and we can remedy that pretty easily, I'm confident, for the future. Anyway, you've got -- the key point is, in the end, not the numbering. You've got the decision for the -- where it says: "Decision for the Serbian people to stay in a joint state of Yugoslavia," have you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Right. Now, just to clarify, and one can see easily from the English version of course as well as from the B/C/S, that this has been -- this is an item on the agenda -- you've just said that yourself as chairman a few lines up and Mr. Zekic is presenting it. So the proposal is that decision: I. On the basis of the right to self-determination and with the aim of a full and permanent protection of rights and interests of the Serbian people, the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina decide to stay in a joint state of Yugoslavia, together with Serbia, Montenegro, Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina, Slavonia, Baranja, and West Srem, and any others who decide in favour of such a survival." So, in fact, Serbian Autonomous Districts is plural, isn't it, there? We've got it singular in the English text, but it's plural. And then II: "This decision takes effect once the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina confirm it in a plebiscite." And then it's to be published in Javnost. And then you -- we can see at the bottom of page 25 in the English. You as the chairman, you say: "Although it's obvious that we need neither to discuss nor to vote on this, we must do it. "Anybody want to discuss it? "No one." You move and so on, and it seems to be adopted "nem con," as one says, and there is applause and so on. And then -- but looking back to what's been adopted, at this point, Mr. Krajisnik, a decision to stay in a joint state of Yugoslavia together with Serbia, Montenegro, and the Serbian Autonomous Districts, this is assuming, is it, at this point something -- well, I assuming that Slovenia and Croatia were going to have no place in the future in Yugoslavia, that they were going to have seceded?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had not seceded yet, but they had already clearly expressed their position that they wished to leave Yugoslavia. And I can explain why this decision was formulated in this way, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, at that point, Mr. Krajisnik, you appear to confirm -- of course, the intentions were very clear from Slovenia and Croatia. I'm just putting it to you that this was you, the Bosnian Serbs, well, accepting what was clearly the writing on the wall that that was going to happen. Correct? You're nodding. We'll take that as a "yes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, without contradiction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm nodding, but I'm -- because I'm waiting for you to be interpreted. But what I want to say is that it was abundantly clear to all of us after all of these discussions held by the president and others that Croatia and Slovenia had serious intentions about leaving Yugoslavia. It would have an anachronous to say at that point that we wanted to live together with Croats and Slovenes if we knew they were about to declare their independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I didn't want to dwell on that point. I just was basically seeking that confirmation that it was recognising the writing on the wall, which you have given. Then -- but you were going to then explain -- beyond that explain why this decision was adopted by the Bosnian Serbs at this point.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. During the distributions from the 10th until the 14th of October, Serb MPs were saying that it was the position of the entire Serb people in Bosnia that they wished to stay in Yugoslavia, even a re-shaped one. And both in the Assembly and outside, they were being told that you don't really have a mandate because many Serbs are speaking up and saying something different, saying that they wanted an independent Bosnia. Your decision, such a decision, would be valid only if confirmed by a plebiscite of Serbian people. That is why we wrote it this way because the volition of those Serb lands elsewhere had already been clearly expressed, those Serb lands that would later become UNPAs, and Serbs in other areas of Yugoslavia. We couldn't include Macedonia, but we included all the others that we could with the proviso that they had to confirm by referendum that it was indeed their desire to stay within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then if we go on -- I hope we're going to find a number 5 in the margin very soon, Mr. Krajisnik. And even better, if against number 5, top of page 27 of the English, we find in the text number 1: "This decision regulates the authorisations ..." Do we have that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Good. And it's all under a heading a few lines earlier: "Decision on granting the authorisation to represent the Serbian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina," and that's what it says again in number 1. And then number 2: "The following are hereby authorised to represent and protect the interests of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina as an item of this decision: Nikola Koljevic to participate in the work of the Peace Conference on Yugoslavia in The Hague." And that -- Professor Koljevic was at that time still a member of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, wasn't he? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And that peace conference -- these peace conferences change their names and the locations all over the place. But for practical purposes, it was a conference under the auspices of the -- or the aegis, perhaps is a better word, of Lord Carrington. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We called it The Hague Conference. It was later followed by the London Conference, but it was actually The Hague Conference led by Lord Carrington.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then it goes on: "And Biljana Plavsic to keep contacts with the representatives of other international organisations and institutions." Now that phrase "international organisations and institutions" covers a multitude of sins, Mr. Krajisnik, but what -- can you say what were the main or the significant organisations that were contemplated there with whom Mrs. Plavsic was to keep contact?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since Bosnia and Herzegovina was going through a crisis, various international organisations were visiting on a regular basis. You know that there was Mr. Cyrus Vance, Mr. Cutileiro, Mr. Wijnaendts, the International Red Cross, UNHCR, many other agencies and personalities were involved, including ambassadors, et cetera. They came regularly to Bosnia, to Sarajevo, so we were informing Mrs. Plavsic that she should formulate our interests in the talks with those agencies and personalities, not leave it to Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And is it correct that Mrs. Plavsic had no -- though being the contact person with the international organisations, played no significant role in the peace negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then we see that Mr. Milutin Najdanovic was to be the person to deal with the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia parliament; Dr. Karadzic with that republic's Presidency; and then you say something laudatory about Mr. Karadzic; and then Mr. Simovic is to have contacts with the Federal Executive Council. Dr. Karadzic we've heard of. Mr. Najdanovic, did he have any other position in the SDS at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Late Milutin Najdanovic was an MP of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the Federal Assembly. We delegated our MPs from Bosnia and Herzegovina to the Federal Assembly, and he was one of them. There were four Serbs represented in the -- representing Bosnia and Herzegovina in the Federal Assembly, so he was representing the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the Federal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But he was being appointed here to represent the interests of Bosnian Serbs in the Federal Assembly. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Mr. Simovic, he was also, was he, a deputy in the Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Simovic was deputy Prime Minister of Bosnia and Herzegovina and at the same time chairman of the ministerial council. That's why he was nominated to represent Bosnian Serbs and to establish a direct link with the federal government of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And if we turn on then, Mr. Krajisnik, to where you should find the marginal number 6, which in the English is at the top of page 31.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Mr. Cancar -- Petko Cancar has been invited to present this item for the scheduling and organisation of the proposed plebiscite. The question is set out in number 2 there: "In the plebiscite, the Serbian people will answer the question: 'Do you agree with the decision of the Assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, 24th October 1991, that the Serbian people should stay in a joint state with,'" and it's the same as we saw before, "Serbia, Montenegro, SAO Krajina, SAO Slavonia, Baranja, West Srem, and all the others who decide to stay.'" And the date was fixed at the 10th of November, 1991. And, Mr. Krajisnik, that's in fact when it happened, on the -- well, on the 9th and 10th, over two days, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then at page 39 of the English, it is -- Mr. Krajisnik, it's item 7, so it's quite a few pages on -- when I say "item 7," it's your marginal note 7, probably half a dozen or more pages on. Do you see that? It will be confusing if I say "item 7," because actually in the text it's right against what is described as item 8. So you've got your number 7 in the margin. It says item 8 in the text, just to keep us on your toes?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "Guests welcome speeches." Mr. Krajisnik, we -- and this is readily checkable, but we've been able to get from another document that -- that that is Mr. Brdjanin speaking here: "I want to move this item without an introduction to discussion." And then: "Dr. President, colleagues and guests," it's Mr. Brdjanin, and he -- some introductory words. And then over the page he says: "Furthermore, as for the plebiscite to be held on 9th and 10th November, I would like to take this opportunity to say that a rally has been scheduled to take place in our town of Drvar, starting at 1400 hours where our entire elite including Mr. Karadzic and others will be present. In Banja Luka a rally will take place," so he's announcing that. But let me just skip, if I may, a couple of sentences. He says: "As a matter of fact, those who think that Yugoslavia should survive are going to come. Those of us here today must say, loud and clear, that we also support the Yugoslav People's Army to carry out their constitutional duties unobstructed, and, as a Serbian Assembly, we must promise to let them carry their constitutional duties. "What does that mean? "No one has the right to call the mobilisation of Yugoslavia's official army, the people's army, private. Therefore, we must say here that we support the mobilisation unconditionally. Why do I say that? Our great leader, and I will not say his name, said that this is not the time of truth, but unfortunately, those who are weaker think that it is the time of force." Mr. Krajisnik, who -- do you -- can you say who was the great leader whose name Mr. Brdjanin could not bring himself to say?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I really have no idea who he meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then he says: "We want the peace in this country" -- can I invite you to read this sentence, Mr. Krajisnik, because we may have a hitch in the English translation. So do you see the next sentence: "We want the peace in this country," could I invite you to read the next couple of sentences from your own language version. Out loud I mean, of course.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We want peace in this country. We don't want borders with anyone, but those who think they can lead us out by force, we have to be ready to prevent that. If, as our people -- I want to say -- or rather, if it should be necessary, God forbid, the sooner this challenge is picked up the sooner the peace will be signed."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the speaker please pick up the previous sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you're invited to go back one sentence and to repeat. And perhaps it's the mistake we all make, that while reading it always goes too quickly. Could you go one sentence back and read it again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. "Today a dream has come true, a dream that had been ascribed to me in the pre-election campaign. People often told me that I said in jest, although I meant it seriously, that Krajina is the west of Serbia. And I explained it this way: It's not possible that people are so ignorant about geography to think that we are in the west, and that's why we have to set our western borders in a way that suits the Serbian people but without prejudice to any other people. "That's all I wanted to say. Thank you very much. "And good luck to you all." This was not written very grammatically and so it was rather difficult. It reads with difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. Now, Mr. Brdjanin, did he have any central role in the SDS at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had no role, apart from being a deputy in the Assembly, and I don't think that he belonged to any of the structures of the SDS either. As far as I can remember. At any rate, he was not an important figure, for sure, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Who was the -- I won't say the next speaker because that's Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik, but the one after that immediately, Mr. Stanko Cvijan, if that's anywhere near the correct pronunciation. Do you see that, Mr. Krajisnik? There's about three or four lines from you and then a Mr. Stanko Cvijan. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the government of Serbia there was a ministry for Serbs outside Serbia, and he was minister in the ministry for Serbs outside Serbia and he attended our Assembly as a guest.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then if we go on then -- I'm not going to dwell on point 8, as it came up in the margin. But if we could go on about four -- about three, four pages, it's actually not a -- there isn't a number in the margin, but do you see the name Mr. Dragan Kalinic comes up for the first time as a speaker. Do you see that, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's at the top of page 47, Your Honours, in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you see that, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And who was Mr. Kalinic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kalinic was a deputy in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina on behalf of the Party of Reformist Forces that was headed by Mr. Nenad Kecmanovic in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And he joined the Serb Assembly because he was an ethnic Serb, and he took part in the debate here as an MP who was an equitable member of the Assembly of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And he --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours, perhaps I just ask for his introductory 20 or 30 lines to be noted, and then pick it up --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Near to what will be number 9 in the margin of your copy, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that's on page 48 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And four lines down, actually, on page 48 there's a reference to the SDA and the HDZ, and the sentence begins: "With this act of establishing an Assembly." Do you see that sentence, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: He says: "With this act of establishing an Assembly which will represent the interests of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, we are today entering a new political reality of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which we have been unable to do through the Council for National Equality and the Chamber of Nationalities on whose establishment we could not agree. The Muslim and the Croatian people have the next move and they will know to choose what suits their interests best. And no Serbian vote should and has the right" -- must be voter, I suggest. "And no Serbian voter should and has the right to be against it." Mr. Krajisnik, when Mr. Kalinic was saying: "The Muslim and the Croatian people have the next move," was that -- was it your view that the next move was in the hands of the Muslim and Croatian people?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would like to explain this in the following way. He meant that we had opted for this path in order to protect our interests because -- let me put it this way. We have -- we did not really have a Council for National Equality, to protect national interests, so we did this in order to protect our interests. And now it is up to you to make your own decision in terms of establishing a body that would protect your interests. Of course, that's not a good thing; it's better if we all reach agreement. But what he said was: Well, this is what we did and now it is for you to resolve your problems, because sometimes your interests will have to be protected in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'm sorry. The Assembly only had the task to meet and debate at that moment on the vital interests of the Serb people. There was a decision that all officials from the ranks of the Serb people from the SDS and others should remain in their positions in the Bosnian and Herzegovinian government. No one had withdrawn, and they were not there to discuss anything else but vital national interests.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And where -- so where Mr. Kalinic was saying: "If they make a similar move," did you understand what he had in mind by "a similar move"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a positive approach by Mr. Kalinic. He said that if they do something similar, and if they establish some council of nations of their own or some Assembly of their own to defend their interests we should respect that. Because at any rate we do not have the right to hold against others what we had done ourselves. It's not that one people has an exclusive right to something. All three peoples have the same rights as far as these very sensitive matters are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then we have quite shortly after that at number 10 in your marginal notes, we have Mr. Koljevic speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not going to dwell on that again, but I -- given Mr. Koljevic's quite significant position, I'd ask Your Honours to note that contribution from Professor Koljevic, Plato rather than Shakespeare in that particular instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then at marginal note 11 but towards the end. Well, perhaps it isn't that near to the end of what Professor Koljevic is saying. He says -- top of page 53 of the English: "It is up to all the patriots who cannot accept that Yugoslavia becomes such a toy." Do you see that, Mr. Krajisnik? Top of page 53 in the English. It's a new paragraph. It's quite a long paragraph. "It is up to all the patriots who cannot accept that Yugoslavia becomes such a toy." Do you ...

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please read it out and then I can give my own comments. I don't even have to find it in the text. I can't find it. I should be able to find the word "Yugoslavia," but I really can't find my way here. Perhaps there's --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll tell you what you might see, Mr. Krajisnik. You might see the figure of 500.000 somewhere around the middle of a quite long paragraph. If that figure jumps off the page to you, that will be the right paragraph. If it doesn't, it doesn't. It's -- I'll carry on, shall I, Mr. Krajisnik? Have a look for the figure 500.000 while you're --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 12/1 -- oh, just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should say I do feel some of this is the -- what I know to be the indirect pressures on all concerned of the very large numbers of Defence teams involved in the cases which have started this week. Your Honour, where that's another matter perhaps we'll take up in other quarters, but my apologies, Your Honour, but it's not going quite as smoothly as it has done.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'm going to carry on with this paragraph you've invited me to read. "It is up to all the patriots who cannot accept that Yugoslavia becomes such a toy to take this moment and from withdrawing in defence of what is disappearing, shift to a constructive action of creating a new Yugoslavia. I see this Assembly, just like those moves we took yesterday in the Presidency of Yugoslavia at the consultations for the change, as a Copernican turn to stop the negative trend of disintegration and start creating a new Yugoslavia which suits us and in which the Serbian people will congregate as much as they can. I would like to remind those who are telling you that Serbs are maniacs who want every Serb to live in one country, that in Croatia alone about 500.000 Serbs will stay in Zagreb and other towns even when we assemble this state. Therefore" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please read slower. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: My apologies, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "Therefore, we are achieving our objective within our abilities, making sure that something is left for the others, as they should not be stripped of their rights. No one has the right to ridicule such an objective of the Serbian people. Of course, our doors are open to the others, although I could quote my faithful fellow sufferer and fellow traveller Biljana Plavsic: Living with Serbs is wonderful, but God it is difficult to wage war with them. "I have adopted this thought of [yours]." Mr. Krajisnik, were you comfortable to associate yourself and would you have associated yourself with those words of Professor Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the late Nikola Koljevic was a poetic soul and he knew how to speak so beautifully. This was a moment when emotions came to the fore. He, quite simply, quoted Mrs. Plavsic here and she was a lot more radical. I'm referring to this last bit. But as for his vision of Yugoslavia, when he referred to that he said, intentionally, implicitly, that we do not accept that someone is telling us that we are trying to create a Greater Serbia and to try to take some lands that do not belong to the Serbs. He was saying -- or rather, Your Honours, at that moment we were deluded. We thought that a new Yugoslavia would not be established, that is to say, it -- consisting of Serbia and Montenegro. Only we thought that our right to remain in Yugoslavia was stronger than the right of those who wanted to secede. But then we realised that Yugoslavia was established, a new one, and we were just left there. So Mr. Koljevic said at that moment that all of us who want to keep Yugoslavia want to remain in a re-shaped Yugoslavia and the door is open to all of those who want to remain in a state that is internationally recognised. And then at this last point he quoted Mrs. Plavsic -- well, that was sort of icing on the cake, but he did not want to make a belligerent statement, especially coming from him. Even if he had said it, nobody would have taken it that way. I am trying to speak slowly, but if the interpreters think I speak too fast, then I am really going to slow down because I want to make their job easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: They usually tell us --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that it is very fast, and for the accuracy of the transcript it would be good if the speaker spoke slower. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your invitation has been taken up, Mr. Krajisnik. Thank you. Your Honour, there's a tiny linguistic point, it did occur to me Your Honours' colleagues might have been entitled to smile at yours and my attempt to dredge up our Latin from many years ago from -- given their languages. But, Your Honour, here the phrase "fellow traveller," in English that does have a distinct connotation of communism.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I just want to clarify it's the -- what appears in the text, and perhaps either you or the interpreters can confirm this, Mr. Krajisnik. What appears in the English text is "fellow traveller." It doesn't have any implication of being a communist here, does it? Just it does in English.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Perhaps it would be best if I were to explain this. We have these two very similar words, "sapatnik" and "saputnik." "Saputnik" is someone that you travel with, a travelling companion; and a "sapatnik" is a fellow sufferer. So then they were together on the Presidency, and they were fellow sufferers. It was hard. She said: He is my "sapatnik," fellow sufferer, because we are struggling together in the Presidency on behalf of the Serb people because we are a minority. These are very similar words, words that sound very similar but that are different, and all the interpreters know that. I think that this says "sapatnik" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Fellow sufferer, notes the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But no, it says "sapatnik" and "saputnik," so it's both I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, that deals with the point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, would this be a suitable moment for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is, Mr. Stewart. Before I adjourn for 25 minutes and announce that we'll resume at a quarter past 4.00. Mr. Krajisnik, the passage Mr. Stewart was drawing your attention to is found on the page which bears the number 12/2, or the ERN number, last three digitals 837, to get you on track again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's most helpful, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, you're invited to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Were Your Honours going to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes, I still owe Mr. Krajisnik -- Mr. Krajisnik, you've requested to speak with counsel on the subject of reports in the media on your testimony which you consider to be unfair in order to see whether or not to address the matter, either through Mr. Stewart or either by yourself. That is the subject on which the Chamber gives you permission to speak with Mr. Stewart during the next break. We have assumed that, to start with, 15 minutes would be approximately what might be needed. So during the next break you have an opportunity to consult -- and you can speak about it with counsel. It's not free to speak with other team members. I take it that you wanted to speak with Mr. Stewart and/or Mr. Josse. So that's the limitation. Not everyone in the Defence -- well, Mr. Sladojevic, in the presence of Mr. Stewart would be no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that's not a general permission for whoever supports and who is on the list of the -- it's limited to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. That's the way we would have understood it, and it's helpful to have that confirmation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the number 12 in the margin should be very shortly after number 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's at the foot of page 53 of the English. Your Honour, I've been invited to go more slowly so Your Honours may notice that I'm going to try and do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's the paragraph beginning: "When the laws fail us, we must not succumb to lawlessness, instead we must create new laws from scratch." Do you see that paragraph, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. "That is how I understand the creation of this Serbian Assembly which was created to defend and legalise the natural rights of a people and not deprive anyone else of their rights." At this stage, Mr. Krajisnik, nine days or so after the crisis in the parliament, this first meeting of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, did you already have it in mind that the Assembly would pass laws in the conventional form, statutes, codified laws, would have a constitution. Was this already part of the conception of this Assembly at this point? [French on English channel].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Assembly had a single mandate -- and it had to do with vital national interests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have a problem with French and English mix-up at this moment, so I don't know whether the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Do you hear the English booth now without any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [French phrase spoken]. Please proceed -- [French on English channel].

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Perhaps you could start again, Mr. Krajisnik. We had a linguistic melange. [French on English channel].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Response to your question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It happened frequently now. Usually the first three or four words are in French and then it switches to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Is it just the English channel now? There seem to be interferences, I see, on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now I hear English only.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Do you only hear English now, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Nevertheless, there seems to be a technical -- let's try slowly to re-start and see whether -- could I ask Judge Hanoteau to listen carefully to the French channel to see whether there's any English on that and let's then can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's one of those rare areas where our resources are greater than the Prosecutions, so any objection is likely to come from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, shall we start again, please, on that. I'll give you the question. Did you all -- the end of my question. Did you already have it in mind that the Assembly would pass laws in the conventional law, statute, codified laws, would have a constitution? Was that already part of the conception of this Assembly at that point?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. That's what I said in one of my previous answers a few moments ago. The mandate of the Assembly was -- well, rather, the deputies would stay in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and then as far as national interests are concerned this Assembly would meet and resolve these vital issues that there was no other way of resolving. There was no Council for the Equality of National Rights or any other body, and at that moment that's what the mandate was of the Assembly of the Serb people in the Assembly in Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was the name of the Assembly then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then the speaker, Professor Koljevic, at the next paragraph he said: "Let me say just two more things, two and a half, rather. As for our first decision regarding the plebiscite, there is often some talk in this town, and there was some yesterday, how the SDS does not represent the Serbian people. That is the SDS that won 90 per cent, more than 90 per cent of votes. Our former partners may think that they would have an easier time with some other Serbs. We are not afraid of the check of our Serbdom, but we rather hope for it after this year of our political work. The plebiscite will be the right answer to all those talks about whether or not we represent the Serbs - it is now up to the people to say." Mr. Krajisnik, at this time in late October 1991, did you have any doubts as to whether the SDS represented the views of the Serbian people of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We, the SDS, firmly believed that we represented the interests of the Serb people. However, there were discussions by the other side that brought that into question and blamed the SDS by saying: You do not have the right to say that on behalf of all the Serbs. And this is what Mr. Koljevic is saying. Now if you remember, I said before this break that in this intermezzo, between the 14th and the 24th, when we had different discussions, and we were trying to find a solution, we were being told: You're not the only ones. There are many Serbs who are calling us by phone and who are in favour of independent states. So what you're saying is not the opinion of the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then if we go on, it's page 67 in the English. It's marginal note 13 on your copy, Mr. Krajisnik. And it should be directly against your own name, just after Mr. Nedic has been talking.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the last page that I have here. Please go ahead. I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. "Ladies and gentlemen. "Today we got our Assembly. The Assembly got its opposition and I hope that we have got some healthy representatives of the Serbian people to protect the Serbian people, deliver their will and implement it in this parliament. "Before I close this first session of the Assembly," and you gave some thanks. And then you -- well, it's easier just to read it through. "Before I close this first session of the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I would like to thank you for taking part in its work and ask you to be the fitting interpreters of the goals and tasks of this Assembly, to fight for the constitutional and legal rights and for the preservation of peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina, to be actively engaged in fulfilling the main objective, not only for the Serbians, but for all the honest peoples and citizens too, to keep a common state which will be a true state, established in a democratic fashion and which her citizens will feel as their own. That would be a state with which all those people who wish to live together will join and where all the citizens will feel free and happy. To all the citizens of Yugoslavia, I wish the war to stop and the peace to come into every home, that the perpetrators of war be punished and that each people remain in Yugoslavia, depending on their choice of state." Mr. Krajisnik, the -- the only war - I'm not suggesting it wasn't more than enough - but the only war that was currently going on at that time was the Croatian war, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: At the end of this first meeting of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, was there, so far as you can say, among those who attended that Assembly, was there satisfaction, dissatisfaction with the meeting and its outcome? What was the overall tone of the reaction of those present?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the overall tone was that everybody was happy to all appearances. But I have to say for truth's sake that when something like this is created there is an aftertaste of misgivings rising from the knowledge that the other two sides are against it. You feel the pleasure that you normally feel when you do something that you believe is right and that you really want to do but that you had to win through struggle, that you had to fight for. So all those present expressed outwardly their satisfaction, but still inside they felt anxiety, knowing that it was a unilateral decision, just like the decisions that the other parties had taken earlier. I don't know if I managed to explain properly the prevailing atmosphere, but also the -- the -- the feelings that they kept to themselves. It was a forced move, if I can put it that way, and that's why it left an aftertaste of anxiety.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it looks as if Mr. Mujanovic has achieved perfect timing with the production of the material. Your Honour, may I just take one second just to sort out the logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have three copies of the B/C/S version marked up in the usual way with numbers. So one for Mr. Krajisnik and then two available for the booth. Your Honours, what we don't have, I'm afraid, in relation to this is the hard copy of the English. Your Honour, could I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, Your Honour. We're moving -- remiss of me. We're moving to the next Assembly session, I beg your pardon, the second session --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could Mr. Registrar tell us -- that would be the second then?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, the 21st of November, 1991. The exhibit number is 64A, 23 -- folder 23, tab 633. Your Honour, we -- we notified these matters, as I understand, earlier in the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although that message might not have come to us, we have a copy now available and on the computer we have one as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I hope we're right, Your Honour, that the procedure for us is to give notification in that way. When something's already been exhibited, we give that specific notification and that's what's required. That's the procedure, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is -- no. Is it 633? No. I make a mistake. I'm sorry. I'll find my copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Binder -- yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, tab --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: P64A, binder 23, tab 633 is what we have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I'll find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And, Mr. Krajisnik, you have the margin-numbered version. So can we go to number 2 in the margin?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's page 7 of the English, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There's a concern it's not marked with the numbers, but we feel confident it is actually.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This copy was probably given to someone else by mistake, the copy you mean. But I'll find the passages that you want. I just don't have those numbers on the margin. I see page number 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It probably repays the investment of time, Mr. Krajisnik, to just sort this out. May I -- may I retrieve that for a moment and then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry, the dog ate my homework is often an excuse that children use. The photocopier ate the last copy with the numbers on, Your Honour; that's what happened in this case. I hadn't appreciated -- my apologies, I hadn't appreciated the three copies I gave were not exactly the same, because I didn't know there had been that photocopier eating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll find our way through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik's copy needs to be swapped over, Your Honour, because, with respect to the interpreters, and my apologies, it is Mr. Krajisnik who most importantly should have the properly numbered version. Thank you. Your Honours have been handed a dauntingly chunky pile of papers there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll manage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sure you will as Your Honours do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, can you find number 2? I don't -- as far as number 1 is concerned, you can ignore that if it's indeed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But number 2, it's at page 7 of the English, Your Honour, towards the bottom of that page Mr. Krajisnik is talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Krajisnik, your name should appear opposite the number 2. Does it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. And you say: "Ladies and gentlemen, I'm convinced that these are crucial times for the survival of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina and I would dare say even more broadly when it comes to the Serbian people as such. Not all of us, however, seem to be aware of this fact; however -- hence what we are doing seems normal and everyday to us. Those who are not aware of their role and the things they are creating should not be criticised but reminded. That is why, gentlemen, I remind you, too, you are the creators of the new history of the Serbian people and not only of Serbian history but of the history of all peoples who live in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Yugoslavia and who want to preserve the state."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But, Your Honours, I don't want to take time on this next bit, but merely draw Your Honours' attention to the fact this is Mr. Krajisnik's contribution at this stage of the discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then if we can go on to beyond -- you should see marginal note 3 following within about a page, page 9 of the English. "This message will never be rendered worthless" is against 3.
