And you say -- not that long paragraph but then -- which I invite to be noted but then the next shortish paragraph you say: "It is normal and in the Serbian democratic tradition, once we created the Assembly of the Serbian people of BH, then we had to be aware - and we were - that the Assembly of the Serbian people of BH came with our own opposition in the same chamber. "I will not praise them too much since they are the opposition - big political opponents to us in government - but on behalf of the Serbian people and myself, I would like to thank them for their work!" Now, there had in the previous Assembly session been some reference to opposition. Mr. Krajisnik, what was the nature and extent of what you are referring to there as the opposition within this Serb Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were MPs of the Serbian Democratic Party and one or two MPs from the Serbian Renewal Movement within Bosnia-Herzegovina. They formed one club. And in this meaning they represented the ruling parties, whereas the opposition were MPs from other parties, from the reformist party, from the League of Communists, and -- I don't know the names of all of them. They were from various parties and members of this Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And was the position that all Serbs who had been deputies in the Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly were automatically invited to become members of the Serb Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the word "invited" may not be the most appropriate, the most adequate, but the door was open to all to participate in that Assembly because they, too, were Serbs and they had the right to have a say when vital interests were decided upon. They had the right for their voice to be heard and be taken into account. Some joined even a year after the Assembly was established. So the door was opened to every Serb in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina to join this Assembly which decided on the vital interests of the Serbian people whenever such issues came on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And that was at that point a qualification as well, was it? You had to have been or to be a deputy in the Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly to have the right to attend and participate in the new Bosnian Serb Assembly, did you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Later on during my testimony we will come to the stage when they wanted to introduce some new representatives into the Assembly, but that failed. All Serbs, and only Serbs, in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina were entitled to become members of the Serbian Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or the Assembly of the Serbian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, you say in that paragraph where you say you won't praise them too much since they're the opposition. And then you say: "Big political opponents to us in government." Were there sharp differences of view between the SDS and members of other parties at that stage?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that stage there were no major differences, only in terms of shades, but that was negligible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, if you go on, it may be over the page, it may be just about a page on in the same page. In the English it's towards the top of page 10 against the line: "We should destroy the bureaucratic approach of the centralised economic power." Do you see that, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then you say: "We have a duty to place every citizen in a state of dependency to make his spending dependent on his income. It is our duty to prevent the outflow of money and unjustified appropriation. It is our goal to decentralise all republican funds, to keep most of the income of citizens and legal entities in their municipalities, regions, and autonomous districts, so that only limited contributions are paid to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Just pausing there. When you referred to "the duty to prevent the outflow of money and unjustified appropriation," what had you in mind by your reference to "unjustified appropriation"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was saying this as an economist, as a trained economist. Bosnia and Herzegovina is an underdeveloped country, and in this underdeveloped country the little resources that were available were all centralised in Sarajevo, where I lived, whereas the periphery, the other provinces, were neglected which gave rise to a certain animosity towards Sarajevo. So our commitment was to decentralisation of those funds in order to develop roads, infrastructure, et cetera, so that the entire Bosnia and Herzegovina would be developed, leaving just a modest amount of resources for the central powers in Sarajevo. It is absolutely not okay to give all resources to the centre. I believe that every state should be polycentric instead of creating this state with a huge head and an underdeveloped body. The entire state is populated, not only the centre; and in today's Bosnia and Herzegovina this is being translated into practice. There are various cantons that are being developed more or less evenly; however, it's year 2006 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Well, there we were here in 1991, Mr. Krajisnik. The next paragraph: "We have a duty to determine the function of regions and autonomous districts with a view to preserving the unity of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is why we should not allow regions to become independent entities, separate from the rest of the Serbian people. It is essential that the Serbian people organisation themselves into one legal and state entity, one common state with all the other peoples who want to build a happier future with us, and gentlemen, you know this but I would just like to emphasise it this time." Mr. Krajisnik, at that point in time in referring to "one legal and state entity, one common state with all the other peoples," what did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was at a time when we had just endorsed the reports of the plebiscite, and we had found -- we had received no positive answer concerning an agreement from the other two sides and we wanted to meet with them and seek a solution because we were clear. Autonomous regions should not transmute into sociopolitical communities, into small states, because our region had 50 per cent of all Serbs in Bosnia. The other 50 per cent or even 60 were dispersed across other regions. We wanted to create a state in which every Serb in this case, but normally every citizen, would be able to exercise, to pursue, his interests. We did not want to please only the Serbian people but to find a solution that would be compatible with the interests of other peoples as well, and that was our purpose here. We knew that we cannot do anything unilaterally. We made an overture to the other two sides, saying that we should adopt a constitution for a Bosnia and Herzegovina that would remain in Yugoslavia and would be acceptable to all of us. And that would very soon become evident once the negotiations start; our position there would be very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, when the phrase there "one legal and state entity, essential that the Serbian people organise themselves into one legal and state entity," were you talking there about an entity that would be recognised as you were accepting was going to happen in the case of Slovenia and Croatia, that would be recognised internationally as a separate, independent, sovereign state?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. At that time we only wanted to rule ourselves within Bosnia and Herzegovina. We didn't want the will of others to be imposed on us. We wanted to stay within Yugoslavia at the time, but that option was very soon afterwards foreclosed because Serbia and Montenegro announced their intention to form a new state comprising only these two republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So by your reference there to "one legal and state entity," what were you contemplating as the territorial extent of that entity?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would later become evident in our decisions. The regions had been established, as I explained yesterday, by the declaration of the will of municipalities. At one point we discussed genocide, et cetera, that's one of the issues here. But leaving that aside, we -- we wanted to form Bosnia and Herzegovina in such a way as to create an entity for Muslims in areas where Muslims were in the majority, a Serbian entity with Serbs in the majority, et cetera. There was no mention of any moves of population. We planned to base our entities on their 1971 census or perhaps a later census, to derive from that information in which areas certain ethnic communities had an absolute majority. But at that time it was already known that a new Yugoslavia would consist only of Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krajisnik, the -- in asking you specifically what you were contemplating as the territorial extent of that entity, and you said that would later become evident, one aspect of that question is this: Did you contemplate at that time that the one legal and state entity into which the Serbian people would organise themselves was -- would lie entirely within the borders of what at this time was Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you also contemplate that it would be less than the whole extent of what at this time was Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't quite understand the question. Maybe I didn't understand the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: First of all, to be clear, Mr. Krajisnik. So you're talking about one legal and state entity into which the Serbian people are to organise themselves. You've just said a moment ago you were not contemplating an entity whose territory went anywhere outside the then-existing borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So the next question then is: Were you contemplating an entity which was less than the whole extent of Bosnia and Herzegovina as it was at this date, 21st November?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that entity was certainly supposed to be smaller than Bosnia and Herzegovina, if I understood your question correctly. The Serbian entity was supposed to be much smaller than Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I understood your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, you have answered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, doesn't that necessarily follow from one of the earlier answers where Mr. Krajisnik said that they would have an entity for those parts where the Muslims were in the majority, and a Serb entity where the Serbs were in the majority, which, if you exclude any foreign territory, would - at least from what my logic tells me - would necessarily mean that it would be more limited than the whole of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, absolutely, my logic is the same as your logic, Your Honour, but I'm not the witness. And Your Honour, what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It may seem oversimplistic to Your Honour, but I'm trying to lay the clearest possible foundation for what I'm then about to ask in relation to the next point. And if it's too clear and is too simple, Your Honour, then my apologies. But my logic is no different from Your Honours', but I've just always felt that erring on the side of having it crystal clear is better. That's all. If I've misjudged it, Your Honour, I've misjudged it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it was crystal clear already to us. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm sorry, may I? There are two overlapping theories here. At this moment we wanted Bosnia and Herzegovina in Yugoslavia, and there were no entities that were supposed to be there. And as I said, later, as it seemed obvious that there would be a Yugoslavia consisting of Serbia and Montenegro only, there was this idea of an independent Bosnia within which these entities would be formed on the basis of the census. I don't want there to be any confusion at this point in time that we wanted some entity which would not be the same entity like in the Cutileiro Plan. These are regions, regions that would have various ties so that the overall interests would be taken into account, not only the Serb interests. So all of that should be taken into account. Therefore, Mr. Stewart was right when he said would it have been less. At that moment, if these regions were brought together they would be a lot less than what Bosnia and Herzegovina was. Of course there would be other regions and yet third regions, but these are regions that had been established earlier on and that had been verified and they would not be sociopolitical communities or states or anything like that. Have I been clear now? I'm afraid that we're going to create some confusion here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There has not been any confusion until now. It was, as I said before, crystal clear. And I just wondered whether that additional question was needed, being it clear already to us. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are going to reconcile me with Mr. Stewart by the end of my testimony. I see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although it's not my objective, it would be a side effect which would not damage anyone perhaps. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm speechless for one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In the transcript the next bit of that sentence, I've already read the whole sentence, but after the reference to the one legal and state entity you then use the phrase: "One common state with all the other peoples ..." Now, the way it reads, Mr. Krajisnik - and please confirm this - is that the one common state you're referring to is the same as the one legal and state entity that you've just referred to. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to read this out. Serbs -- well, like the Germans have Bavaria that is called a state and then in the United States of America there is Texas that is a state, well, this is what was meant here, not an independent state but that it should be -- well, as far as I can see it -- or actually, I cannot see it. It would be easier if I could find it here now. But it does refer to Yugoslavia. It's Serbs and other people who would live in that state. Yes, yes, exactly. The interests of all peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina; yes, you're right. Yes. That's the part that you referred to, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So on the footing that what you're referring to is one legal and state entity, same as what you're referring to there as one common state. Your reference to "one common state with all the other peoples who want to build a happier future with us," what is meant there by "all the other peoples"? Does it -- I'll be more specific. Is that intended to embrace Serbs and non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certainly referring to both Serbs and non-Serbs here. But I have to say that it is very difficult to interpret what this speaker here is trying to say because Yugoslavia and Bosnia are being mentioned here intermittently and then this entity. Now I'm speaking on my own behalf. The intention here was for us to create something that would be in the interests of the Serbs and the non-Serbs. Now, when he's speaking here, there's that part of the sentence that you referred to, autonomous regions that would be linked-up --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, may I just interrupt for one moment, Mr. Krajisnik. There is no -- there is no confusion here, is there? We are all understanding, are we, that the speaker here is you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I just wanted to be clear about that, Mr. Krajisnik. You used the third person and you referred to difficulties in interpreting. I just wanted to clarify that. I'm -- I beg your pardon. I interrupted just to make that crystal clear at least.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at another paragraph where I said that it is our duty to determine the function of regions and autonomous districts with a view to preserving the unity of the Serb people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Therefore, we should not allow regions to become independent entities separate from the rest of the Serb people; that is to say, that they should not become states. Deputies, you know that, but I am just pointing out here that we have to do this. Let us not turn the regions into states because that was the inclination of the Serbs -- or at least that's the way it was. They wanted small regions that they established to turn into states so that they would be, as I said yesterday, little Napoleons, that is to say small-scale emperors. That's the point of this whole idea. Because a lot of Serbs --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I guess -- perhaps I'm wrong here. I guess that you are probably going a bit fast for comfortable interpretation. Maybe I'm wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Interpreters, am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm not wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: You're not wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. That's crystal clear as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, this is -- as you've acknowledged yourself, this is a difficult area. It's rather technical, it's rather difficult. In your own interests, as much as everybody else's, I think the slower the better here.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for having cautioned me. I want to indicate what I said at the beginning of this paragraph. The point is that I, as the speaker, am referring to a danger looming over the Serb people, that regions could behave like states, which would lead to multi-fold danger. Then I emphasised that in the past Serbs were -- tended to divide themselves up and to set up statelets. It was necessary for us to unite because outside these regions there would be a lot of Serbs left in other parts that were not these regions. We kept saying that. If there is to be any unification, it would have to be at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It would be a chamber of peoples or whatever. And then all Serbs would be involved in that kind of organisation. If it would only be the regions that were to be linked up, that would mean that you'd have several tiny statelets within a confederation of regions. That is the gist of what I was saying. This speech refers to that phenomenon within Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'll go a bit more directly to the point that arises out of your reference to a common state there. The one legal and state entity -- the one common state that you refer to there confirmed by you as the same thing you're referring to, that would be, wouldn't it, essentially a Serb-run entity. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. An entity with a Serb majority. Those are the regions involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And so when you refer to "one common state with all the other peoples who want to build a happier future with us," are you referring there to the other peoples who -- the non-Serbs who would continue to live within that Serb-run entity, or are you referring to other peoples outside that Serb-run entity?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean that a constitution should be made for this Serb entity, but I'm calling it that only conditionally. However, in that constitution it should say that there should be a segment within a common constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It would be easy for you to see that later, that we make this for us and then it's within the joint constitution for Bosnia-Herzegovina, too. That's what you said, too. In this constitution and in this common state, if we are to call it that, without the actual characteristics of a state, all of those who wish that we all together build that kind of state should live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, again, the rest of that -- well, the next few paragraphs, they're not unimportant, Your Honour, by any means, but they're not giving rise directly to questions now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then you've got point 5 in the margin of your copy, Mr. Krajisnik, I think against a paragraph that begins: "Gentlemen, if we are out-voted ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's at the top of page 11 of the English, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's a shortish paragraph, that three-line paragraph beginning: "Gentlemen, if we are out-voted in discussions of national interest ..." It should have the number 5 in the margin very close to it.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. It says: "Gentlemen, if we are out-voted in discussions of national interest to the Serbian people at the institutional proceedings, the will of the Serbian people will be expressed through the decisions of the Assembly of the Serbian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Your reference to "institutional proceedings," you're referring there primarily, are you, to the Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If we are out-voted in Bosnia-Herzegovina - and that only has to do with vital national interests - then we're going to discuss it at this Assembly and the decisions of that Assembly will be valid. It's not democratic out-voting but an out-voting that violates the constitution, and it's very important to distinguish between the two. It is democratic to have MPs out-vote each other but not to violate the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you refer then -- the next paragraph you say: "The basic principle we should observe in our activities is not to impose the will of the Serbian people on other peoples. We should represent the legitimate will of the Muslims and Croats, but we must not underestimate our advantages expressed through the realistic ratio of political forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina." What were those advantages, as you saw them?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lawyers kept advising us to the effect that we have an advantage because we are within Yugoslavia and that that is a right that supercedes the right of those who wish to leave Yugoslavia. So that's the advantage. Later on we established something completely different, but at that moment it was supposed to be an advantage for the Serb people that Bosnia-Herzegovina was in Yugoslavia, and that is the substance of this part of my remarks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then the next paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours, I'm not going to dwell on the next paragraph but it's important as part of this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then at the bottom of page 11 of the English, and it's at a paragraph beginning: "On this occasion, too, I should remark ..." Do you see that short paragraph, Mr. Krajisnik? It's three lines.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. "On this occasion, too, I should remark that there is noticeable rivalry and disunity in some municipalities. All forms of desire for power should be dismissed. We have always lacked unity, and now we need it more than ever." The "we have always lacked unity," "we" is a reference to Serbs, is it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you've remarked about "noticeable rivalry and disunity in some municipalities." How -- what was the degree of disunity and what was the degree of difficulty it was creating?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many examples of rivalry at municipal level and other levels, and then these rivals would create problems for each other. They would be laying blame at each other's door and of course there can be no progress if there is that kind of rivalry. I'm talking about people who are in power in municipalities. That is the only organisational unit that existed, apart from the republic itself. And this primarily refers to Serbs because I did say that it was about Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were any steps being taken at this time to try and dampen down such rivalry and heal such disunity?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic was the president of the party. These cadres only came from the SDS, from the party. And very often, himself, went or sent his representatives to these municipalities to try to bring about some kind of reconciliation in order to find a solution. He also had the right to dissolve Municipal Boards of the SDS. So there was this ongoing activity in order to bring about reconciliation, and sometimes people were also replaced by others. I'm talking about party affairs now. Of course members of Assemblies, since they belong to political parties, too, most often carry through these decisions that were agreed at party level. So efforts were made to resolve the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you talked about -- well, you mentioned Mr. Krajisnik [sic] going or sending his representatives to municipalities to try to bring about some kind of reconciliation?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Karadzic, Dr. Karadzic, it's -- my second reference to Krajisnik should be Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you talked about Dr. Karadzic going or sending his representatives to municipalities to try to bring about some kind of reconciliation. Did he on any occasion during 1991 send you as his representative to any municipality for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall two cases. Once, as president of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I went to Sekovici. That is a purely Serb municipality, and it was the municipal organs that were quarrelling, and it was a state problem, so to speak. And I remember this other situation, I don't remember exactly when it was, when there was a problem between the political party and the municipality in Trebinje. And Mr. Karadzic asked me to accompany him in order to find a diplomatic solution, in order to bring about reconciliation, but we did not succeed. I remember those two examples, but perhaps I attended a similar meeting in Banja Luka or somewhere else with Mr. Karadzic. But I do not remember any other situation when I was sent on my own. I beg your pardon. There was this other problem, too, in Drvar. I remember that. A delegation from Drvar came to see me as president of the Assembly. They were quarrelling over some municipal affairs, and then I resolved the problem autonomously. It was not a party problem but a state problem. I received the delegation, so that was my mediation, so to speak, but it really had nothing to do with the party. That is as much as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So -- just on this point, Mr. Krajisnik, you've mentioned that you went to Sekovici -- sorry -- have I --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sekovici, Trebinje, and I mentioned Drvar, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you in the course of 1991, in the course of your work or duties or responsibilities in the political field, visit any other municipalities outside Sarajevo in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a private problem on account of which I did not travel because my wife had been ill. I don't remember whether I visited some municipality. Maybe I did, but that was as president of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Or perhaps -- I remember a problem being mentioned here of a meeting in Doboj and then the question was put whether I was in Doboj or not, that is towards the Autonomous Region of Doboj. At that time I did attend that meeting, and I will explain that. However, if I did this, it was very, very rarely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, your last question suggested - at least from what I -- how I interpreted that - that the four events Mr. Krajisnik mentioned were all in 1991. That had not been established yet, but perhaps you could seek confirmation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, Your Honour is -- is absolutely right about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, those -- all those visits that you have just mentioned were in 1991. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drvar was in 1991. Sekovici was in 1991. I just can't remember when this happened in Trebinje. I can't remember that exactly, whereas the two I mentioned were in 1991 for sure. I think that Doboj was also in 1991. I cannot remember the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If Trebinje was not in 1991, was it in 1992 or in 1990? Do you see what I mean? Was it later than 1991 or earlier than 1991, if it wasn't in that year?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Absolutely it only could have been 1991 or perhaps 1992. And 1990? No. I did not go to any municipalities in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If we go back to the transcript that we were looking at following on from the paragraph we just looked at --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Stewart. If you ask me whether I visited some municipality in 1990, was that your question? My understanding was whether I visited some municipalities in 1991 when I was president of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, it would have been my question but you already answered it because you said you didn't go to any municipalities in 1990. That was going to be my next question --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But since you answered it before I asked it, even I don't need to go --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- any further, Mr. Krajisnik. So going back to the transcripts, the paragraph we'd looked at on this occasion, too, I should remark -- we're going to move on from that -- that's just the reference point then. The next paragraph is -- well, it's: "Deputies!" In the English at the top of page 12. And then it says: "We can send a message to all the people in Bosnia and Herzegovina." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "We can send a message to all the people in Bosnia and Herzegovina that we want to preserve Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole and as a part of Yugoslavia, because only in a whole Bosnia and Herzegovina and Yugoslavia can all the Serbs, and other peoples, too, live in a single state. If anyone should want to separate Bosnia and Herzegovina from Yugoslavia, he must bear in mind that he will have the entire Serbian people against him." So, Mr. Krajisnik, is this correct. The position is that everything that you were saying a couple of pages previously and that I was asking you questions about, about the Serbian people organising themselves into one legal and state unity, that would only ever arise if this wish to preserve Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole and part of Yugoslavia failed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. I had emphasised that that was the second stage. Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then you continue: "One cannot fight against a people or secede. It is not worth starting something knowing that it is doomed to failure. "It is our wish to live together, but in harmony and love. But if we cannot live together, it would be ruinous to wage war. It would be better to separate. Gentlemen, I would like to paraphrase our former brethren, the Slovenes - 'let's separate so that we can associate again.'" And that separation that you were referring to then, it would be better to separate rather than wage war, that's the separation inherent in what you were saying about organisation into a -- one legal and state entity. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me to just give a brief introduction to this. In all versions that envisaged the Serbian entity, I was absolutely against any borders separating the three peoples because nobody was closer than these three communities. And if we were unable to find a -- I mean, a mutually acceptable solution, then I don't know. We were telling them: The Serbian people had their own plebiscite. They expressed their will. Don't go against it, otherwise you would have a -- you would be faced with a secession. It's better to negotiate, it's better to agree. Any borders separating us would be a disaster. Even if it were physically possible to create borders, it would be against all of our interests. That is the meaning of my words here. And when I invoke the Slovenes, they had said: Let us separate so that we can get together again, something to that effect. Their -- these words were some kind of political marketing, meaning that they wanted to dissolve Yugoslavia in order to establish some other ties. My opinion was that borders made no sense among communities that were so closely knit. That was the meaning of my words. And the answer to your question is yes, but I had to explain it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's -- well, I'm entirely in Your Honour's hands of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn for 20 minutes and re-start at five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I should report briefly on the particular --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it -- it concerned media reporting of this -- in fact, television reporting of these proceedings in Sarajevo. Mr. Krajisnik has expressed on one or two specific points considerable concern about the way in which his evidence and the current state of these proceedings is being reported an a television channel which he is himself able to see, because in the United Nations Detention Unit some of these channels are made available. Your Honour, Mr. Krajisnik, I'm sure, as we alive to freedom of -- freedom of expression, freedom of the press, and the inevitable in real-life inaccuracies that occur from time to time; however, he's concerned beyond that normal margin which just has to be accepted as part of life. Your Honour, we're really a little bit in Your Honours' hands as to how one should proceed. The -- these concerns does suggest -- they do merit investigation. The first thing to do is really to find out perhaps exactly what was said so that one can form some view. We wonder in the circumstances, Your Honour, whether this is a matter that perhaps the Registry might pursue in the first place. It's an unprecedented problem, as far as we're concerned, Your Honour, here. We don't know the procedures and the normal way, if there is a normal way, of dealing with the matter, but that might be an appropriate course. We could give information on the problem to the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whether it's an unprecedented problem, Mr. Stewart. Better reporting on court cases whether in this Tribunal or anywhere else is not unfamiliar to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, Your Honour, absolutely. And we discussed that very point with Mr. Krajisnik, and we're all, Mr. Krajisnik and we are aware that that's a part of life. Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll certainly get in touch with the Registrar himself to see whether -- what position has been taken until now by the Registry. And as far as this Chamber is concerned, I will discuss the matter with my colleagues soon, but I would not give any false expectations as to a Chamber interfering easily in reporting on cases that are before it because it would require an assessment of the fairness not of its -- on trial but of the reporting on it. And even if you would consider it unfair, the freedom of expression, as we all know now and then, leads to what others would consider unfair. So therefore, I don't want to give any false expectation. The only thing I'll -- I'll say that I'll get in touch with the Registrar, report to him that the issue has been raised here, and ask him whether there's any -- what, until now, the attitude has been of the Registry, whether to refrain from any comment or whether to more actively, perhaps, support fair reporting. Of course, I have not seen it, so I have got no judgement at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, me neither.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to say that on the basis of what Mr. Krajisnik has raised. And the other thing is I'll discuss with my fellow Judges whether there is -- whether anything should be done or whether we should not do anything. And I'll discuss that and I'll very briefly report to you on the outcome of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I mention one specific point, if Your Honour may or may not think it suitable to raise with the Registrar. There are -- the way the matter is conducted here, there are two possible channels of information that go to the television station. One is that they can be simply watching the trial on the internet. That's an obvious one. The other is that there is some source and channel from within this building. It's really got to be one or the other, effectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. From what I know that every television station which is interested in receiving the recordings of this Tribunal is -- gets it for free, although there is a delay of half an hour, but it's accessible to whatever television station, from what I understand, and without any payment. So therefore I would say that the -- that's one of the guarantees of the public character of our trials is that all the video -- apart, of course, if it's closed session, but it's made available to the outside world. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. We understand it entirely, Your Honour. We certainly don't seek to challenge or undermine that in any way, far from it. But we -- the only question that remains then is whether there is -- separately from that whether there is any sort of briefing given -- because, after all, this institution does have a -- as we understand it, has a press department, so we simply -- well, that is one of the other possible sources of information. And without pre-empting and without criticising anybody in advance who may or may not be involved, it is necessarily, therefore, if it's a source of information, it's at least, in theory, a source of inaccurate information. But I'm not saying in advance, Your Honour, that is the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. From what I know is that the press releases that are issued by the -- by the office are -- may I just finish for a second - are public. You can find them on the web site as well. What other information is given, I'm not aware of it, but I'll certainly pass that portion of your remarks to the -- to the Registrar as well, because the press office has a different name, but our press office is --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- is under the responsibility of the Registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour might just remember that a long time ago, about two and a half years ago when this trial began, right at the very outset there was an issue raised by the Defence of concern as to an inaccurate report - and it certainly was in that case an inaccurate report in one of the leading English newspapers - where the information certainly did come from within this building. It died a death and nothing was done about it. But, Your Honour, that -- it's always a possibility, and we remember that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we have official sources, and I could not for the full 100 per cent exclude that unofficial sources from wherever could play a role as well. Mr. Krajisnik, you wanted to add one thing, I take it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I can be of assistance to Mr. Stewart. I'm not complaining about the reporting of the press; it's their trade. In the Detention Unit I am able to watch one TV station called Hajat, a TV station from Bosnia-Herzegovina. And for two days running they reported in a completely distorted manner what I have been saying here in the courtroom. There is one trial here, but there is also a media trial in Bosnia. It's not the same thing as the coverage of the Guardian or the Washington Post or some other such newspaper. I would like to tell you exactly what my problem is in a private session. I have frequently been under attack from the press and that is completely normal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll discuss with the other Judges whether -- to what extent we'll go into the matter and whether we would do that in a public session or in a private session. We'll give you our views on that -- at least the result of our -- of our conversations on the matter, our deliberations on the matter, soon. Yes. Then, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. A small matter, Your Honour -- well, small, not unimportant to Mr. Krajisnik, but there's one aspect of what he told us which he doesn't wish, and reasonably enough, doesn't wish to be ventilated in public. Your Honour, in the first place what we propose is that we would raise that in an e-mail which we'd copy to the Prosecution, of course, in the usual way. It's a relatively narrowly confined aspect of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: An e-mail of the type you indicated will be read by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Returning to the 2nd Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly that we were looking at. We're at page 12 of the English transcript, and it's the passage we were looking at before the break, Mr. Krajisnik, where you had said: "It is our wish to live together but in harmony and love. But if we cannot live together it would be ruinous to wage war." You see that paragraph, do you? It is just a reference point, Mr. Krajisnik, so we can work from there. Do you see that paragraph? You end up saying: "Let's separate so that we can associate again."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. If we go on then, three paragraphs from that -- no, two paragraphs, you say: "On our way to achieving the goals of the Serbian people we accept all friends, we accept everybody except traitors and opponents. "Traitors and outcasts are the most difficult opponents. We would like to send the following message to all those who falter or are neutral, weak, or misguided and who do not feel like traitors: 'Today you still have time, tomorrow will be too late.' "Join us in creating a common state and you will be proud that you are not state destroyers, but state creators." Mr. Krajisnik, did you have in referring to "traitors," did you have any particular people or group of people in mind?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I talked about that kind of people I always have specific persons in mind. In every ethnic community there are such people, and likewise at that time there was Serbs who were greater opponents of Serbs than even the most radical Croats or Muslims were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What -- in this particular context at this particular time, what position, in your view, on the part of a Serb constituted treachery?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to be quite specific. If it is obvious that the constitution has been violated to the detriment of the Serbs, and if one of the Serbian MPs from whatever party rises in parliament and propounds a totally opposite view for some purely private reasons, the private reason being that under the previous system which had a system of proportionate representation from which that person benefitted, those people always had it better than some other people who could never actually come to the fore, even if -- even though they would have represented Serb interests much better than those actually occupying the posts. They were actually working against Serb interests.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, would you turn on to number 6 in the margin of your copy which is in the middle of page 15 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then we see a paragraph beginning: "The Main Commission for the plebiscite of the Serbian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina at its meeting in Sarajevo on 11th November 1991 reviewed the reports of the municipal committees for the plebiscite on results of the plebiscite of the Serbian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina held on 9th and 10th November ... in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina and stated the following ..." And then figures are given that a total of 1 million, then 64.157 citizens were registered, and then just going down to the figure at the bottom, a total of 1.162.032 citizens of Serbian nationality voted in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and of those 1.161.146 voted in favour, 398 voted against, 488 were invalid. Had you been expecting a result of that nature and scale before the plebiscite?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those were approximately the results, although they are on the optimistic side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you mean they were better than you had expected when you say "on the optimistic side"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Slightly better than we had forecast.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, the results are set out in some detail here in figures. I'm certainly not going to dwell on those, but would invite Your Honours to note them, and they include results from outside Bosnia as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May we go on, Mr. Krajisnik, to where you would find number 7 in the margin.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Which, Your Honours, is at page 25 of the English, where a decision is to be proposed by the vice-president Dr. Milanovic. And the propose is that the -- "based on the will" --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you find that, Mr. Krajisnik, Dr. Milanovic speaking? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: He says: "Mr. President, ladies and gentlemen, members of the Assembly, dear guests. Based on the will expressed by the Serbian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the plebiscite held on 9th and 10th November 1991 and the conclusions of the Assembly of the Serbian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina adopted on 24th October 1991 and on 21st November 1991, the Assembly of the Serbian people for Bosnia and Herzegovina hereby adopts the following." And: "Decision." And number I is: "Municipalities, local communes, and settlements where the plebiscite was held of the Serbian and other peoples to remain in the common state of Yugoslavia together with the Republic of Serb, Republic of Montenegro, the Serbian Autonomous Districts," again it must be plural, "of Krajina, Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem was held on 9th and 10th November 1991 where more than 50 per cent of the registered citizens of Serbian nationality voted for a common state, and where citizens of other peoples and nationalities voted to stay in the common state of Yugoslavia shall be considered the territory of the Federal State of Yugoslavia." Mr. Krajisnik, we can easily infer, can't we, from the fact that there are applause, and then all deputies rise, long applause, that that gained immediate and enthusiastic approval? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- well, let's -- let's read the next bit first. Number II: "Parts of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina from item I of this decision, together with the territory of the Republic of Srpska" -- Serbia, I beg your pardon, "the Republic of Serbia and the Republic of Montenegro, Serb Autonomous Region Krajina, SAO Krajina, SAO Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, make up the core of the common state of Yugoslavia." And then III: "Municipalities, local communes, and settlements in which the plebiscite was not held may vote in a new plebiscite or based on the decision of the Municipal Assembly may remain in the common state from item I of this decision or may be organised in a different way." So, Mr. Krajisnik, going back, then, seeing those elements together, but going back to number I, the result, as stated, of this decision would be that where "more than 50 per cent of the registered citizens of Serbian nationality voted for a common state," that municipality, commune, or settlement was to be considered the territory of the federal state of Yugoslavia. That's plain from the wording, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So, for example, is this correct: That if the Serbian -- if the Serbs in a particular municipality were in a minority and that municipality as a whole -- but if more than half of them had voted for a common state, then logically their municipality was to be considered territory of the federal state of Yugoslavia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this requires an explanation. A plebiscite is a way of -- is a way for a people in one territory to express its will. In this case, wherever Serbs had declared their will in one territory to stay in Yugoslavia, that area was to be part of Yugoslavia. But the next article deals with exactly how this was going to be arranged. The first article just notes that the Serbs in a particular territory had expressed their will to stay in Yugoslavia, but it doesn't mean -- it doesn't mean that it will be so, because negotiations with the other two sides have yet to begin. There is a huge difference between a plebiscite and a referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could you, Mr. Krajisnik, explain what you see as that huge difference between a plebiscite and a referendum.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A plebiscite has the purpose of establishing the will of the people in one area and, once expressed, this decision of the people has to be verified, or ratified, by the Assembly. But if you hold the referendum, like it was done in Bosnia, then it's a final decision with executive force. It has to be enforced. In our situation, we had adopted at a referendum a decision that was contrary to the plebiscite. The Muslim side made a completely contrary decision, saying that Bosnia has to be independent. And that's the basic difference between the plebiscite and the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So -- because, Mr. Krajisnik, the terminologies are used in all sorts of different ways and all sorts of different places, and so on. But as far as you are using those terms, it's essentially this: A referendum you regard as binding then on the other political organs? That's the -- the people have spoken. They've given an answer to the referendum, and that's got to be implemented. Is that -- that's your summary of a referendum, is it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A referendum was held in Canada, in Quebec. If that vote had won 51 per cent, it -- Quebec would have become an independent state. In our state, if you have to express your opinion whether you want taxes raised or something else, then you just get the opinion of the people. We wanted Serbs to tell us whether they wanted to stay within Yugoslavia, and we got their opinion. In all areas that were polled, those people wanted to stay within Yugoslavia, but in order for their decision to be implemented there had to be negotiations within Bosnia and Herzegovina, with the other two ethnic communities, and that's the way it goes. Later, in 1992, a referendum was held and that decision had to be implemented. That's the difference between the way this operation was carried out by Serbs, on the one hand, and Croats and Muslims on the other. I don't know what difference there exists between the terms in other foreign languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the problem. You have clearly explained what you consider to be a plebiscite and what you consider to be a referendum, whereas in many other countries they would use it in different ways. You would have a consultative referendum, for example, which means just consulting the people. But you make a difference between consulting the people or to give the decision in the hands of the people, who would then, by majority, make that decision. And the last you called a referendum.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest that whenever the issue is further raised that it should always be clear whether we are talking about consultation of the people or whether we are talking about a decision made by a vote of the people by majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour, and I'll do my very best in any questions to be clear. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Terminology --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- is seeing well that I had in mind that we would talk about the question of whether it would be a binding referendum or a non-binding referendum. That's just precisely how it might operate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me one moment, I know Mr. Josse wants to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So let me give you the hypothetical example, Mr. Krajisnik - you may say it's not hypothetical - that I had mentioned a few minutes ago. So in a situation -- say you've got a municipality, municipality X. Municipality X where the Serbs are in a minority but there has been this plebiscite conducted in that municipality among the Serbs and more than 50 per cent of the Serbs have voted yes in this plebiscite for a common state. Under the literal terms of part I of this decision, their municipality is to be considered the territory of the federal state of Yugoslavia. That's how it would literally apply, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If Serbs were a minority in that municipality, there are smaller administrative units called local communes. And if that area had held a plebiscite, then it had to be territorialised in some way. We didn't have the right to say: This area belonged to Yugoslavia if Serbs were in a minority there. There are many towns where one ethnic community was in a majority but overall speaking throughout that area in terms of the land register another ethnic community was the majority. So if Serbs were the absolute, so to say, overall majority in that area, then that area would be considered part of Yugoslavia. It was not enough for Serbs to be a majority just in one little unit. That's why there is a difference between maps based on land registers that we proposed and one map that was produced here by a witness who explained that those were maps until municipality. I believe it was Witness Okun. That was an important difference. And whenever we negotiated, we used maps based on land registers. Within one municipality you could look at one smaller unit or at the municipality or area overall. I don't know if I managed to explain this clearly enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can I ask you about point III or part III of this decision, the one that starts: "Municipalities, local communes, and settlements," this is top of page 26 in the English. Do you see that, Mr. Krajisnik, we read it a few minutes ago: "Municipalities, local communes, and settlements in which the plebiscite was not held" --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And they went to a -- "may vote in a new plebiscite or based on the decision of the Municipal Assembly may remain in the common state from item I of this decision or may be organised in a different way." That phrase, "may be organised in a different way," was that intended to be just entirely general or were specific, alternative ways of organising themselves actually in contemplation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is precisely the question that I have just answered. Local communes within municipalities where Serbs were overall in a minority also had to declare their will. And this phrase, "organised in a different way," if that municipality did not take part in the plebiscite, whatever they said, whether they wanted to stay in Yugoslavia or not, it was up to them to decide how they wanted to be organised. The plebiscite was over. We knew who was in favour of staying in Yugoslavia, whereas the rest had to state their opinion. This was an opportunity for those who did not take part in the plebiscite to make it plain what they wanted. The plebiscite was only for those who were in favour of staying in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, part IV, which we haven't read yet. Then part IV that follows on: "Dr. Radovan Karadzic, Dr. Nikola Koljevic, Dr. Biljana Plavsic, Momcilo Krajisnik, Dr. Aleksa Buha, and Dr. Vojislav Maksimovic, as representatives of the Serbian people, are authorised to negotiate with representatives of the Muslim and Croatian people on the organisation of the future common life in the territory of the present Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. "In negotiations with the representatives of the Muslim and Croatian people, the representatives of the Serbian people from the preceding paragraph shall recognise the interests and national decisions of other nations in regard to which community they wish to live in, and they may be opposed to the Muslim and Croatian people forming separate state entities or a common state." Now, the question I'm going to ask concentrates on that last bit, Mr. Krajisnik, that they -- this is an authority given to them, clearly. "They may be opposed to the Muslim and Croatian people forming separate state entities or a common state." By reference to "separate state entities," did that mean the equivalent for Muslims and Croats of that single state entity that we considered a while before the last break, the Serb entity that had been under discussion? Was that the equivalent?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was written by lawyers, and lawyers tend to complicate even very simple matters. This was supposed to mean: We are not imposing our will on other people. Let them organise themselves as they wish. Let them state their wishes as they please. We have stated their opinion -- our opinion, now you state yours. When the American administration came to support the union between Muslims and Croats, that became evident. Nobody should impose their will on anybody, and even this additional sentence that can now be interpreted in various ways, the crux of the matter was that they -- it was up to them to decide what they wanted and we were not going to tell them what to do. I meant Serb lawyers. I didn't mean lawyers in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course I was not going to jeopardise our respect to reconciliation, Mr. Krajisnik, by commenting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would not mind, Mr. Krajisnik, and I would not even contradict that there is no merit at all in it. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm not saying a word, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, can we go to marginal number 8 in your copy, which is the top of page 28 of the English. Just to note, in fact, the fact that the -- it records: "The Assembly unanimously adopted" -- I beg your pardon, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, is that 6 or 8?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: 8, yes. It's not much further on. It's about a page and a bit, possibly, further on. It's -- simply, it's in capital letters in the English. But it's simply to -- to note that: "The Assembly unanimously adopted the decision on the territories who decided in the plebiscite" --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I'm sorry. I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That -- well, that's just to note that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then about a further page on, number 9 in the margin: "Decision on the verification of the proclaimed Serbian Autonomous Regions in Bosnia and Herzegovina." And that --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that this passage: "The Assembly unanimously adopts the decision about territories that have stated in the plebiscite they were staying in Yugoslavia"?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That was the first passage - that's exactly right - against number 8, Mr. Krajisnik. It's just to note that. Yes. And then number 9, moving on about probably a page, I think, something like that. And then it's -- in fact, it's Dr. Branko Milanovic who is putting forward this -- well, it's a draft decision that he's putting before the meeting, a decision on the verification of the proclaimed Serbian Autonomous Regions and the -- it says: "Decisions on the proclamation of the Serbian Autonomous Regions in Bosnia and Herzegovina are hereby verified," that's the proposal. And they are: "Autonomous Region of Krajina," and then all the municipalities are listed. I won't read them out, Mr. Krajisnik; too painful for everybody. And then about six lines down: "The Serbian Autonomous Region of Herzegovina." And then about three lines down in the English certainly, on page 29: "The Serbian Autonomous Region of Romanija and Birac." And then three lines on in the English: "Serbian Autonomous District of Semberija." Another couple of lines on: "The Serbian Autonomous District of Northern Bosnia," and then the municipalities are listed. And then Part II: "The Serbian autonomous districts on the previous item are part of Bosnia and Herzegovina as federal units in the common state of Yugoslavia." And then III: "Rights and obligations," and so on," are to be regulated by a separate decision." And then IV: "The status of the municipalities in the city of Sarajevo and parts of the city of Sarajevo" --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I haven't got these two pages here, that's why I'm a bit confused. I have page 31 and then page 33 of the text. That's why I don't have the other part.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You might have been confused, Mr. Krajisnik, my fault, by my reference to page numbers in the English, which probably doesn't correspond to your own language --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note we have the same problem. It's 31 and then 33 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's just the other way around. It's first page 33 and then 32. So it's just that it has to be put back. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would this resolve the problem --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is it that the pages are just in the wrong order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Swapped, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- for you, Mr. Krajisnik

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what Mr. Krajisnik told us and that's what the interpreters told us, too, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I was trying to follow it here as well, Your Honour. Oh, yes. Okay. Got it. Right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And so then do you see part IV then of that draft decision: "The status of the municipalities in the city of Sarajevo and parts of the city of Sarajevo in which the Serbian people are a majority shall be determined by a separate decision." You see that Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. IV is -- oh, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was it contemplated at that time that that was a separate decision which would follow quite soon, or was it that the complexities affecting Sarajevo would probably require a very considerable time to sort out?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sarajevo, from the very outbreak of the crisis, was a separate problem. And to the end of the war it was always on the agenda, so to speak. I can say that in most proposals there was the proposal to transform Sarajevo into two wholes, not to divide it as some people have imputed, but two parts where there would be municipalities with a Serb majority and a territory with a Muslim majority. Two-thirds would belong to the Muslim majority municipalities and one-third to the Serb majority municipalities. And that is why it was stated here that the question of Sarajevo would be resolved in due course because that was the most painful issue of all. Every agreement envisaged that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it seems something may have been omitted in the translation. Mr. Sladojevic suggests to me that there was a reference to the inner city in that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, did you make some specific reference to the inner city in the course of your answer?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did not mention the inner city, the centre of the city. I talked about Sarajevo, that it would be transformed into two wholes, so it would have been different than it was before. Of course, Pale was always excluded because they had reached a decision to become a separate entity as a municipality that was on the outskirts of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, could you explain, when you talk about two-thirds -- you talk about two separate -- into two wholes. Two-thirds would belong to the Muslim majority municipalities and one-third to the Serb majority municipalities, but you say that that wasn't dividing it. Could you explain in what way an arrangement under which two-thirds would belong to Muslim majority and one-third to Serbs is -- but was not a division.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Sarajevo was always divided into municipalities. So it wasn't ever a single whole. We called for a different transformation because there were many Serbs and Serbs were not in power anywhere. They were a minority everywhere except for Pale and Ilijas, and we called for the establishment of smaller municipalities because there was some municipalities with a population of 150.000 people where these local problems could be resolved. Now, why is this not a division? If you remain within Bosnia, then there's no division. It can simply be as if that municipality belongs to one entity or the other. I'm talking about all plans where it had been envisaged to have a solution for Sarajevo that two-thirds of this Sarajevo without Pale should belong to the Muslim/Croat entity, the Muslim/Croat side, so to speak, and one-third would belong to the Serb side. And you have that in every agreement that was reached. Until that is reached -- now, why was I saying all of this? The UN, the United Nations, administration was supposed to be there until a solution is solved because it was impossible to resolve the issue of Sarajevo together with all of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Mr. Owen described this the best in his book "The Balkan Odyssey." You can see the maps there and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could you turn, please -- it's quite a long way on, Mr. Krajisnik. It might be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, if you are moving to another subject, I'd rather spend the last couple of minutes on the -- in private session. Mr. Krajisnik is invited to remain here, but then again as an accused to follow the -- but I would --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour, I am. Of course. No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I think D171 and 173, if I'm well -- if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm not sure we're going to need to go into private session because my learned friend Mr. Harmon tells me he has no objection. We've discussed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, nevertheless -- was that -- I think it was a document where the Chamber would not have major difficulties in --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Clearly if the Chamber needs reminding of the contents, then we will need to go into private session. We're in -- well, I'm in Your Honour's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What we also could do is to see whether the parties agree on the matter. If that is the case, then the Chamber of course will look closer into D171 and 173 and whether it could follow the parties in this respect. If not, we would revisit the matter and then in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Of course I'm content with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had no objection to both of those exhibits being under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll look at the matter, and we'll give either our decision to you or we'll revisit the matter in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll finish for the day. Mr. Krajisnik, the same instruction which I will repeat quite many times in the future not to speak with anyone about the testimony already given or still to be given. We'll adjourn until tomorrow, quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon. And we'll be in Courtroom I tomorrow. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 28th day of April, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.
